tutorial_example_entry.lesson_title: Solving Transform Problems Using Known Pairs
tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Solve continuous-time Fourier transform problems by decomposing the signal into known transform pairs and selecting the appropriate property to assemble the resulting spectrum.

sections.lesson_title: Solving Transform Problems Using Known Pairs
sections.section_title: Introduction to Solving Transform Problems Using Known Pairs

blocks.text: The solve order in this lesson is simple: identify the closest known pair, rewrite the signal so every modification is visible, and then apply the property that matches each visible change before combining the pieces. The goal is not to start from the transform integral; it is to reuse stored pairs and the properties attached to them.
Start with the clean base case. If the signal already matches a known pair, you can read the spectrum directly. If a constant multiplies that pair, carry the constant through by linearity.
The same idea extends to sums. Rewrite the signal term by term, transform each known-pair piece, and add the results.

For shifts, scaling, reversal, modulation, and differentiation, do the same thing in a slightly different order: first rewrite the signal so the modification is visible, then apply the matching property to that rewritten term. The rewrite tells you which factor or spectral change belongs to each piece.
That is the pattern you will reuse in the next steps: one known pair, then one small rewrite, then the property that matches it, and finally the combined spectrum.

sections.lesson_title: Solving Transform Problems Using Known Pairs
sections.section_title: Identifying the Base Fourier Transform Pair

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the decaying exponential multiplied by $u(t)$, which matches the stored transform pair for $e^{-at}u(t)$. Start by recognizing that base pair, because the only new feature in this example is the constant weight 4 in front.
Substitute $a=2$ to get the transform of the base signal $e^{-2t}u(t)$. Then carry the outer factor 4 through by linearity; the scaling does not change the transform shape.
So the final spectrum is $X(j\omega)=\frac{4}{2+j\omega}$. This is the model for the next examples: match the known pair first, then carry any visible modification through the appropriate property.

sections.lesson_title: Solving Transform Problems Using Known Pairs
sections.section_title: Decomposing a Signal into Known-Pair Terms

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a sum of two decaying exponentials multiplied by $u(t)$, and each term already matches the known pair $e^{-at}u(t)$. The move here is to split the signal into terms before doing any transform work.
Write the signal as two separate known-pair terms: $e^{-t}u(t)$ and $2e^{-2t}u(t)$. Then transform each term on its own and carry the coefficient on the second term through by linearity.
Add the two spectra to get the final result. The important step is the decomposition: once the sum has been split into known-pair pieces, the transform is just the sum of the individual transforms.

sections.lesson_title: Solving Transform Problems Using Known Pairs
sections.section_title: Selecting the Property for Each Signal Modification

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a delayed copy of the same one-sided exponential pair. Rewrite the signal as $3x_0(t-1)$ so the delay and the scale factor are both visible before you transform anything.
With the signal written as $3x_0(t-1)$, the property choice is automatic: apply linearity for the factor 3 and time shifting for the delay of 1. The delay contributes the phase factor $e^{-j\omega}$.
Substitute the base spectrum into that shifted form and simplify. The result is the original rational spectrum multiplied by the phase factor from the delay.

sections.lesson_title: Solving Transform Problems Using Known Pairs
sections.section_title: Combining Multiple Properties on a Modified Known Pair

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a known exponential pair that has been delayed and then multiplied by a cosine. Rewrite the signal as $2x_0(t-1)\cos(3t)$ so the two modifications are visible before you transform anything.

First apply the delay to the base pair: $x_0(t-1)$ has spectrum $e^{-j\omega}X_0(j\omega)$. Then apply cosine modulation, which turns multiplication by $\cos(3t)$ into two frequency shifts. The outer factor 2 cancels the $1/2$ from the cosine rule.
Now substitute $X_0(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$ into each shifted copy. Keep the two terms separate so the delay phase and the modulation shift stay attached to the correct copy.

sections.lesson_title: Solving Transform Problems Using Known Pairs
sections.section_title: Assembling the Final Spectrum from Transformed Pieces

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a sum of two known-pair pieces: one composite term from the previous example and one plain exponential. Rewrite the signal as $x(t)=x_1(t)+x_2(t)$ so you can transform each piece separately and only add the spectra at the end.

Use the previous chain for $x_1(t)$: its spectrum is the sum of the two shifted copies from the delayed cosine-modulated exponential. For $x_2(t)$, direct lookup gives $e^{-t}u(t)\leftrightarrow\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$. Then add the results.
Now assemble the full spectrum by linearity. Nothing new happens in this step: the final answer is just the transformed composite piece plus the transformed simple piece.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Base Fourier Transform Pair

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the decaying exponential multiplied by $u(t)$, which matches the stored pair for $e^{-at}u(t)$. The only extra feature is the outer factor 5, so first identify the base pair and then carry the coefficient through linearity.
Substitute $a=3$ and attach the coefficient 5. That gives $X(j\omega)=\frac{5}{3+j\omega}$.

The cue is still the one-sided decaying exponential, so it matches the same base pair $e^{-at}u(t)$. The negative coefficient stays attached to the spectrum by linearity; it does not change the decay constant.
Substitute $a=4$ and keep the factor $-2$ in front. The transform is $X(j\omega)=\frac{-2}{4+j\omega}$.

sections.lesson_title: Solving Transform Problems Using Known Pairs
sections.section_title: Decomposing a Signal into Known-Pair Terms

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Split the signal into the two known-pair terms $e^{-2t}u(t)$ and $-3e^{-4t}u(t)$ before doing any transform work. Then apply the pair $e^{-at}u(t)\leftrightarrow \frac{1}{a+j\omega}$ to each term and carry the minus sign through by linearity.

Adding the two spectra gives $X(j\omega)=\frac{1}{2+j\omega}-\frac{3}{4+j\omega}$. The key step is the decomposition: once the sum is split into known-pair pieces, the transform is just the sum of the individual transforms.

The signal is already a sum of two known-pair terms, so split it first and keep the negative sign on the second term. Then use $e^{-at}u(t)\leftrightarrow \frac{1}{a+j\omega}$ on each piece and add the spectra.
So the final spectrum is $X(j\omega)=\frac{4}{1+j\omega}-\frac{1}{3+j\omega}$. The move is still decomposition before computation, not collapsing the time-domain terms into one expression.

sections.lesson_title: Solving Transform Problems Using Known Pairs
sections.section_title: Selecting the Property for Each Signal Modification

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Write the signal as $4x_0(t-2)$ with $x_0(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$. Linearity keeps the factor 4, and the delay of 2 contributes the phase factor $e^{-j2\omega}$.
So the transformed signal is the base spectrum multiplied by the scale factor and the delay factor.
Rewrite the signal as $2x_0(t+1)$ with $x_0(t)=e^{-5t}u(t)$. The factor 2 stays outside by linearity, and the advance by 1 gives the phase factor $e^{j\omega}$.
That means you use the shifted version of the known pair, not the unshifted one.

sections.lesson_title: Solving Transform Problems Using Known Pairs
sections.section_title: Combining Multiple Properties on a Modified Known Pair

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Rewrite the signal as $2x_0(t-2)\cos(5t)$ with $x_0(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ and $X_0(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$. Apply the delay first, then use cosine modulation to split the spectrum into the $\omega\pm5$ shifted copies.
Substitute the known pair into each shifted copy and keep the two terms separate so the delay phase stays attached to the correct frequency shift.
Rewrite the signal as $2x_0(t-1)\cos(4t)$ with $x_0(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$. The delay contributes the phase factor, and cosine modulation splits the spectrum into the two shifted copies.
Substitute $X_0(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$ into each copy and simplify. The correct answer keeps the delay factor attached to each shifted frequency term.

sections.lesson_title: Solving Transform Problems Using Known Pairs
sections.section_title: Assembling the Final Spectrum from Transformed Pieces

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Split the signal into the delayed cosine-modulated piece and the plain exponential piece. Transform each part separately, then add the spectra at the end.
The final spectrum is $X(j\omega)=X_1(j\omega)+X_2(j\omega)$. The step is only assembly: keep each transformed piece intact and combine them at the end.
Split the signal into the delayed cosine-modulated term and the decaying exponential term. Transform each piece separately, keeping the minus sign on the second piece.
The final spectrum is $X(j\omega)=X_1(j\omega)+X_2(j\omega)$. Assemble the transformed pieces at the end and do not shift the unmodified exponential term.
